title: Reel two opening; Depression food, red beans and cheap groceries
summary: Reel two is announced, then Matassa explains growing up in a grocery during the Depression and how cheap beans and salt meat were.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Okay, well, alright. I've got to finish doing now. I've got to take this thing. Alright, we forgot to billboard the last one. This is an interview with Cosmo Matassa. My name's Tad Jones, and it's May 28, 1993. This is reel number two, and we've got to go back and billboard reel number one. And we're at Tulane University at the Jazz Archive. Okay, that's out of the way. Okay. So, speaking of food, how was the food growing up? I mean, we think about people in New Orleans eating red beans and rice, and here's a big Italian family. Okay, wait a minute.

Two things you've got to remember. I came up as a small child during the Depression. I was fortunate enough for my folks on the grocery store. So I was spared the problems other people had. You know, what do we eat today?

Yeah. So, in that sense, I was really lucky. I was very lucky. But there was not a lot of sharing, a lot of caring. Families tended to take care of family, that kind of stuff. And my father and mother, I know, on occasion did what they could to help somebody that they knew needed help. Right. Generally, the biggest single thing, and it seemed to happen regularly enough, as I became old enough to be aware of it, was people who were in very modest economic means having children, new babies. New babies. Right. That was always a time of joy, but also a real problem. And I can remember my mother being involved in that kind of stuff, you know, putting together a little package of stuff for somebody who just had a baby. And like I say, I was lucky. I didn't want in that sense. And although things were tough, food was, by today's standards, ridiculously cheap.

And you've probably heard the old thing about Quatti beans. Maybe you haven't, I don't know. No, no. Tell me about it. For 10 cents. 10 cents? For 10 cents, you could go to the grocery store and get a little package of beans and rice, and a little black pepper and another piece of paper wrapped up like that, for a dime. You could get a piece of salt meat for 15 cents, a pretty big hunk of it. And what was that called? Salt meat, that's, it was called Quatti, which is a kind of half partial thing, you know, normally you would buy a pound of beans, but if you didn't have enough money to buy a whole pound, you could buy this lesser amount of beans and rice and be able to cook them in. And the red beans became famous for Mondays because Mondays was wash days. And red beans are something you could cook without having a stand and watch it all the time.
You just go over and stir it every now and then. Did you have standard food every, I mean, on this day was this meal, and this day was this meal?
